# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Right after I typed how my people follow a conversation today, it makes sense that Keel shows me how that went, on a scale, before testing whether it falls short.
screens.why2: 'Followed everything', 'caught only the gist' and 'missed most of it' are how my users and I talk about a table conversation; nothing needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know these outcomes first-hand from my co-founder's '20% at best, nodding along' and from our users' testimonials, so I can judge the rungs from my own world.
screens.why4: The five rungs run cleanly from all to none on how much was followed, don't overlap, and leave no common last time without an answer.
screens.why5: The rungs keep my measure, how much of the talk was followed, and the act stays a face-to-face conversation with hearing people, with nothing about glasses or captions leaking in.
screens.why7: There is one measure (share followed) and five rungs best to worst; the first works and the last fails outright; the line after 2 leaves two working rungs against and three shortfalls for, so the belief can be supported or refuted; the stranger's escape is I can't recall, which is right for an act that can't be handed off.

screens.why1: Choosing who will put the questions to people is a natural last step before the link goes out by text.
screens.why2: Two names, a play button, a price in credits and a note that the questions are also on screen: I can follow all of it on first reading.
screens.why3: I can listen to two five-second clips and pick one, which is entirely within what I know and can do.
screens.why4: Both choices are voices, but most of my people are deaf or hard of hearing, so the choice I actually need is missing: captions or text first, with the voice off or secondary, and the hint only covers this in passing.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is changed or leaked here; it is only about who reads my questions.
screens.instead: Who should ask them your questions? Daphne / Saskia / Text only, with no voice (my people are deaf or hard of hearing), with captions shown under the video by default.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is natural to choose how my respondents answer, just before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words: 'read and tap', 'talking, typing or tapping', and 'pick Daphne or text' are clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know my users well: many deaf and hard-of-hearing adults prefer text, and some do not speak, so I can answer this at once.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and mine is there, but they all assume speech. The AI option opens with 'asks aloud' and 'speak into it' as its draws, and there is no way to answer in ASL, which some of my Deaf respondents would want (the Andrea Whitlock kind).
screens.why5: It keeps my actor wording exactly and leaks nothing about the glasses or captions to the respondent.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? — Read and tap (type or tap, no sound needed) / Daphne on video with every question captioned on screen / Let them choose; plus a note that no answer needs speech.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how people answer, the last thing before sending is who gets the link, so this screen belongs here.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own term I haven't seen yet in this flow, and the options switch between 'I send' and 'you send'.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching hard-of-hearing people I've met by name or posting in an HLAA chapter group or a deaf community forum, so I can answer this from my own work.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people (named contacts, a Keel search list, an open link in a community), with nothing silly or missing.
screens.why5: Nothing about AirCaps or the wearer role leaks, and my pick of named people with their own links is kept as I made it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People Keel finds for me (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already gather, like an HLAA chapter or a Deaf community forum)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated, but the number beside it, a median of 4 days, sits inside my 4-to-7 band and reads as if the belief held; the number that actually decides it (4 of 7 against a bar of 5, one short) is only down in the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: The tally of 3 holding and 1 split over 7 people is plain, but the Frequency card stacks the split, median, below, at-or-beyond and bar into one dense line, and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I had to read twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency 4 to 7 days, keeping the thread as one of the top two, and today's way falling short are my beliefs in my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what the split on frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether the wedge is people who have hard conversations every day or whether to price for occasional use; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card, but nothing says that seven people is a small base for 'deaf and hard-of-hearing adults', and the 'Holding up' labels read as settled.
screens.instead: People disagree on frequency: 4 of 7 lose the thread on 4 or more days, one short of the 5 you needed; the other 3 have it 2 to 3 days a week. That is only 7 people, so check whether your daily wearers are a narrower group than all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults before you size the market on everyday use.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells, all for me, on a 0 to 7 axis with my bar marked at 6, so what is counted, out of how many, and where the bar sits are clear at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The belief 'At least 8 in 10 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days' is my band, my people and my problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' tells me the problem is widespread in my wedge, and it points me to the next two cards for how often it happens and whether it matters, which is where the stage page's Frequency disagreement lives.
screens.why_b5: n is visible everywhere, and '7 of 7' is hedged as 'a small group: a lean, not a call' and 'among these 7', so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: Drop the trailing '— the most recent time it happened' from the Asked line; the gate is a plain yes/no, and that tail belongs to the story question after it.

screens.why_b1: 'People disagree' sits right beside 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 days, against a bar of 5 of 7 and '1 short', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The count, the 7 people and the bar marker at 5 are plain, but the axis starts at a 0 nobody could pick, the median is printed twice, and the legend's 'what you said' and 'at what you said' sit next to the list's 'inside what you said', so I had to look twice to match cells to labels.
screens.why_b3: Frequency, '4 to 7 days out of 7' and 'lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people' are my range and my circumstance in the words my customers use.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points me onward but doesn't say what a 4-to-3 split means for my wedge, such as whether my low of 4 days is too high or whether the people below it are occasion-led users (theatre, seminars, a noisy walk).
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly calls 7 a lean, not a call, but the Asked line's tail 'the most recent time it happened' suggests a single-occasion question when the item counted days, which misstates what people answered.
screens.instead: Drop 'the most recent time it happened' and start the axis at 1; say 'Your low of 4 days sits exactly on the middle answer: 3 of 7 lose the thread on 1 to 3 days, often around one event such as a theatre visit or a seminar, so ask whether your wedge is the everyday group-talker or the occasional big-room user before setting the range at 4 to 7.'

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 put it in their two and the bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the strip with its marker at 5 read at once, but the caption says each of 7 picked two while the bars add to 13, so I had to stop and work out that one person picked only one.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Keeping the thread of the conversation, with the four rows I listed and the circumstance I typed, are what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly says top two, not first, but stops there; it doesn't tell me that the thread is the pain to build around or that Getting a word in, the runner-up at 3 picks, points at the 'join' half of my job.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays on the screen, the count line calls it a lean, not a call, and the So line refuses to claim it ranks first, so nothing goes beyond these seven.
screens.instead: 7 people · 13 picks (one picked only one) -- all 7 put keeping the thread in their two; getting a word in came next with 3, so joining in, not only following, is worth a look.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that clears the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts per rung over 7 people, with my line drawn under 'Missed only a little' and the strip's marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits read at once; only the count line's 'one of the two worst outcomes' takes a second glance, and that is not the chart.
screens.why_b3: My job was 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation'; the card says 'following what hearing people said in the conversation', which I recognise but which drops the joining half and is Keel's phrasing, not mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' names the gap (gist or missed most) but stops short of saying what that means for the glasses, such as having to get people from the gist to nearly all of it in group settings.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and every claim matches the seven answers listed.
screens.instead: Say what to do next: 'Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, mostly at the gist or worse; on the next study the glasses must move people from the gist to nearly all of it, and in group conversations, where it fell short.'

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' is my dimension, but the belief line drops the 'join' half of my job, 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation', and is phrased awkwardly; it is recognisable but not quite what I typed.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for AirCaps; the 'When a line fails' heading even frames a held line as a failure, and I get no next step about the one holdout or the Frequency split.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, but the 'When a line fails' heading over a held line is a small mislabel, and nothing says that 7 people is a thin base.
screens.why_b6: Tomás, who is deaf on one side and gets by with the end seat, shows me that people with single-sided loss may already have a workaround good enough to skip my glasses, which is a segment edge I did not write down.
screens.instead: Held, 6 of 7 (a small sample): the one holdout is deaf on one side and manages by choosing his seat, so ask whether single-sided loss belongs in your day-one wedge.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually got lost in one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: 'Lose the thread' is exactly how I'd describe it when people talk too fast or over each other and I miss where it went, so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost track of a conversation at work, at dinner or at the store in the last week; it's my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, captions or the company reaches me; it only asks about something that happens to me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with 'Yes or no' after it, easy to catch in one go.
screens.why7: It asks about the part that hurts, losing the thread, not the routine of talking with hearing people, so someone who followed every conversation this week can truly say No and I can say Yes, within the 7-day window and with no escape.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to losing the thread this week, asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Losing the thread of a conversation with hearing people is exactly how I would put it, and days out of the last 7 is easy to count.
screens.why3: I know which days I was at work, at the shop or with family and missed what people were saying, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer for someone who already said yes, and I can't recall sits apart as the only escape.
screens.why5: It uses the same words as the gate question and shows nothing of any product or the founder's terms for people like me.
screens.why6: It is one short question, then say a number from 1 to 7, then the one escape, which is easy to hold on first hearing.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the window, running 1 to 7 with the unit said once, the escape I can't recall is apart, and losing the thread is an act that happens on a given day.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which of the hard parts of these conversations I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: Two options talk about me as 'they' ('their hearing loss', 'where they can see every face'), so I had to read them twice; 'their hearing loss' even sounds like the hearing people's loss.
screens.why3: Telling people I'm deaf, picking a seat, keeping up and getting a word in are all things I do in every conversation with hearing people.
screens.why4: Choosing a seat where I can see every face is how I keep the thread, not a separate hard thing, so it overlaps with that option; the 'they' and 'their' wording is not how I'd say it.
screens.why5: The third-person 'they' and 'their' read like someone describing deaf people from outside rather than asking me, though nothing of a product shows.
screens.why6: Four short options and one escape are easy to hold, but 'telling the people there about their hearing loss' is a mouthful when heard, and it's unclear whose hearing loss is meant.
screens.why7: The own row 'Keeping the thread of the conversation' is there, not first, with three rivals and 'None of these' at the first ask, but the seat row is a means of the own row and the card says it should have been put aside.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Telling people I'm deaf or hard of hearing · Keeping the thread of the conversation · Getting a word in at the right moment · Asking people to repeat themselves · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread and what I'd most want made easier, it makes sense to ask how much of that last conversation I actually followed.
screens.why2: The stem is clumsy: 'How did following what hearing people said in the conversation go?' needs a second read, though the options are words I'd use myself.
screens.why3: How much I caught of my last conversation is something I always know, and usually painfully well.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from everything to nothing without overlap, 'caught only the gist' is exactly how I'd put it, and 'I can't recall' fits a conversation nobody else could follow for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or a company's plan shows; it's just about following a conversation.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list I can hold, but the stem is a long, roundabout clause that's hard to take in on one hearing.
screens.why7: Every rung is one measure, how much I followed, from a working rung through to failing outright; the line after the first two leaves rungs for and against the belief, and the required 'I can't recall' escape is present.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed everything that was said · Missed only a little · Caught only the gist · Missed most of it · Could not follow it at all · I can't recall

typo_leaks.text: How far back should deaf or hard-of-hearing aduts look for the last time a conversation with hearingg people is too fast or too noisy to follow?
